claims.text: The laser-induced thermionic-emission method produces ultrafine high-entropy nanoalloys with diameters of 1–3 nm.
The resulting nanoparticles have equiatomic, well-mixed elemental distributions.
The initial nanoalloys possess a disordered atomic structure.
Laser-induced thermionic-emission reduction forms high-entropy nanoalloys on a defective carbon support.
Slow reaction kinetics in conventional synthesis promotes phase segregation in nanoalloys.
Nanosecond laser synthesis provides sufficiently rapid reduction to overcome immiscibility and segregation during particle formation.
Rapid cooling after laser synthesis kinetically freezes a disordered atomic arrangement.
Kinetic trapping occurs before significant atomic diffusion can take place.
The defective carbon support anchors or stabilizes metal atoms in the nanoalloys.
Interactions with defects in the carbon support inhibit metal-atom mobility.
Rapid kinetic trapping and defective-support interactions act cooperatively to slow diffusion and phase segregation.
This cooperative mechanism suppresses chemical ordering and structural rearrangement at elevated temperature.
Laser-synthesized nanoalloys on defective carbon will retain a single-phase, chemically homogeneous structure during high-temperature annealing.
Conventionally synthesized nanoalloys or nanoalloys on non-defective supports will exhibit more chemical ordering or phase separation under identical annealing.
Conventionally prepared nanoalloys typically begin segregating or chemically ordering when heated under the proposed conditions.
The predicted stabilization applies to particles smaller than 5 nm.
The predicted stabilization applies up to approximately 0.5 times the melting temperature.
Above the stated size or temperature boundaries, diffusion-driven segregation may overcome kinetic trapping and support interactions.
